Most historic premillennialists accept the late date, citing Irenaeus, who says the vision was seen near the end of Domitian's reign. They read much of Revelation and part of the Olivet discourse as still future, with a final tribulation before the return. Many see AD 70 as a near fulfilment that foreshadows the final one.

A late date means Revelation cannot be about AD 70, so its tribulation, beast and judgments remain future. Dispensationalists read 'this generation' (Matthew 24:34) as the generation that sees the signs, or as the Jewish people. A future great tribulation is essential to their sequence leading to the millennium.

Jesus offered the promised Davidic kingdom to Israel. Israel rejected it, so the earthly kingdom was postponed. The church age is a distinct period, not the kingdom foretold by the prophets. Christ will set up the literal kingdom on earth when he returns, and reign from Jerusalem for a thousand years.
Christ alone, by his personal return in power. Human effort cannot bring in the kingdom; it comes suddenly, from heaven.
Preach the gospel, gather the church, live in holiness and watch for the Lord. Good works and mercy are commanded, but they are not building the kingdom.
Culture is not expected to be Christianized before the return. The age ends in apostasy and judgment. Christians do good where they can, as salt and light, without a program to transform society.

It takes the Old Testament promises to Israel at face value. It keeps the church focused on the gospel and on hope in Christ's coming. It guards against confusing any political order with God's kingdom.

Critics say the 'postponed kingdom' idea fits poorly with texts where the kingdom has already arrived (Matthew 12:28; Colossians 1:13). Some say it has encouraged withdrawal from public life and a pessimism that neglects the cultural mandate.

Defenders answer that classic dispensationalists affirm a present spiritual rule of God and a 'mystery form' of the kingdom now. They point to strong records of missions, hospitals and relief work. Holding the future kingdom as future, they say, is faithfulness to the text, not pessimism.

Christ's Davidic reign has already been inaugurated: he sits at God's right hand on David's throne. The kingdom is present now in a spiritual form through the Spirit and the church. The earthly, national kingdom with Israel restored comes at the return, in the millennium, and then in the new creation.
Christ inaugurates the kingdom by his resurrection and ascension, and completes it at his return. The church shares in its blessings now but does not complete it.
Witness to the reigning King, live as a community of the new covenant, and do justice and mercy as signs of the coming kingdom.
Social and cultural good works are real foretastes of the kingdom, but full justice and peace on earth wait for Christ's return.

It honours both the 'already' texts and the future promises to Israel. It brings dispensational theology closer to the wider scholarly consensus on the kingdom while keeping a future for national Israel.
Classic dispensationalists say it blurs the church-Israel distinction. Covenant theologians say that if the Davidic throne is already fulfilled in heaven, a later earthly fulfilment is not needed.
Proponents answer that fulfilment comes in stages, so a present heavenly reign does not cancel a future earthly one. Peter in Acts 3:21 still looks for a 'restoration of all things' at the return.

The kingdom is God's dynamic reign. It broke into history in Jesus' ministry and is present now ('already'). It is not yet consummated. At Christ's return his reign will be visibly displayed on earth in a millennium, and then completed in the new creation.
God, through Christ. The kingdom is God's act, not human achievement. Believers enter it and serve it, but Christ consummates it at his coming.
Preach the gospel of the kingdom to all nations, live as a people of the age to come, and show its power in healing, mercy and justice.
Christians engage culture as signs of the kingdom, without expecting the world to be won before the return. Evil and good grow together until the harvest.
It joins present kingdom power with future hope. Ladd's 'already and not yet' framework is widely used across the views. It has deep roots in the early church fathers.
Amillennialists say a millennium after the return adds a stage that the rest of the New Testament does not mention. Postmillennialists say it is too modest about the gospel's power in history.

Historic premillennialists answer that Revelation 20 most naturally follows the return in Revelation 19. They hold that the New Testament expects suffering and growth side by side, so modest hope is realistic, not defeatist.
Anabaptist / kingdom-community

The kingdom is present now in the church as a visible alternative society. The church does not try to run the state. Instead it shows the world a different way of life: forgiveness, shared goods, peacemaking and love of enemies. The kingdom will be completed when Christ returns.
Jesus, through his cross and resurrection. The church does not build the kingdom but receives and embodies it.
Be the church: a faithful community that lives by the Sermon on the Mount, refuses violence, and witnesses by its common life.
Not withdrawal but distinctiveness. The church serves its neighbours and speaks truth to power, while refusing to use the sword or the state to impose the kingdom.
It takes the ethics of Jesus seriously as social ethics. It avoids the dangers of state religion. It explains why a small, faithful community can be a powerful witness.
Critics say it neglects Christian callings in government, law and business, and can leave public life to others. Some ask whether pacifism is required by the New Testament.
Proponents answer that the church's first political act is to be the church. Christians can serve widely, but their deepest loyalty and method are shaped by the cross, not by control of society.
Amillennial two kingdoms

Christ already reigns. He rules his church as Redeemer through word and sacrament, and he rules the world as Creator through common providence. The redemptive kingdom is present now in the church. Culture, politics and work belong to a common kingdom shared by believers and unbelievers until the return.
Christ, who already reigns from heaven. The kingdom is received, not built (Hebrews 12:28). It will be revealed in fullness at his return.
Preach the word, give the sacraments and practise church discipline. Believers serve faithfully in their callings in the common kingdom.
Christians should work with excellence and justice in culture, but culture is not redeemed or Christianized as such. The church as an institution does not take political positions beyond Scripture.
It protects the church's spiritual mission from political capture. It gives believers freedom in their callings. It builds on Augustine, Luther and older Reformed teaching.
Neo-Calvinists say it divides life too sharply and limits Christ's lordship over culture. Some say it can make Christians passive about injustice.

Two-kingdoms writers answer that Christ is Lord of both kingdoms, but rules them in different ways. Believers must act justly in every calling; the claim is only that culture is not the church's redemptive mission.
Amillennial neo-Calvinist (Kuyperian)

Christ is Lord of every square inch of creation. Redemption restores creation, it does not escape it. Believers therefore work in every sphere (family, science, art, politics, business) as the renewal of creation. They do this in hope of the new creation at Christ's return, not expecting to complete it before then.
God, who renews creation through Christ. Human work matters, but the full kingdom comes only with Christ's return. Some fruit of faithful work may be carried into the new creation.
Preach the gospel and form believers who serve Christ in every calling. Each sphere has its own God-given authority, and the church does not rule the others.
Strong cultural engagement. Christian schools, unions, political parties and scholarship are fitting expressions of Christ's lordship. Hope rests on the new creation, not on cultural victory.
It gives a theology of work and culture rooted in creation and new creation. It avoids both withdrawal and theocracy through 'sphere sovereignty'. It has inspired wide Christian scholarship.
Two-kingdoms critics say it confuses common culture with the redemptive kingdom. Others warn that 'transforming culture' can drift into a political program or a confident triumphalism.
Neo-Calvinists answer that they expect antithesis and suffering until the end. They are amillennial and do not promise victory in history. They work in culture because Christ already owns it.

Christ reigns now from heaven and will put all enemies under his feet before he returns. Through the Spirit-blessed preaching of the gospel, most of the world will be converted. A long era of peace and righteousness will follow, and then Christ will return.
Christ by his Spirit, through the gospel. Postmillennialists stress that the victory is God's work by ordinary means, not human achievement.
Make disciples of all nations: preach, baptize and teach obedience. Expect the nations themselves to be discipled over time.
Culture will be increasingly shaped by Christian faith as people are converted. Social change flows from conversion, not force.
It takes seriously the growth parables and the scope of the Great Commission. It was the view of many Puritans and of leaders of the great missionary movement. It gives strong hope for history.
Critics point to texts of growing evil before the end (2 Timothy 3:1-5; Matthew 24:12) and to the violence of the twentieth century. They say it can tie hope to visible progress.
Postmillennialists answer that history moves slowly and with setbacks. The church today is far larger and more global than in the past. Texts of evil describe particular times, not the whole age.
Theonomic Christian Reconstruction

God's law, including the moral and judicial laws of the Old Testament as applied in the New, is the standard for individuals, families, churches and civil governments. As the gospel spreads, societies will be reconstructed on biblical law. It joins postmillennial hope with this view of law. It is controversial, and many postmillennialists reject theonomy.
God, through regeneration by the gospel. Reconstructionists insist the change is from the bottom up, through conversion, not imposed by revolution or force.
Preach the gospel, teach the whole law of God, build Christian families, schools and institutions, and call rulers to obey God's law.
Culture and civil law should be brought under God's revealed law over time. Proponents differ on how far Old Testament civil penalties apply today.
It asks a real question: if not God's law, what standard should rulers use? It is consistent in applying Scripture to all of life. It has spurred Christian schooling and home education.

Critics across the views, including many postmillennials, say it misreads how the Mosaic civil law was tied to Israel's covenant, and that some penalties would be oppressive today. Others warn of theocracy.

Theonomists answer that they reject force and expect change only as people freely believe. They say the New Testament changes the law only where it says so, and that every society enforces someone's moral law.
Kingdom Now / Seven Mountains

Teaching linked to the New Apostolic Reformation (NAR). Believers are called to take dominion and bring God's kingdom into seven spheres of society: religion, family, education, government, media, arts and entertainment, and business. Proponents frame this as influence and servant leadership, led by present-day apostles and prophets. It is widely criticized by evangelicals of all millennial views.
Believers empowered by the Spirit, often led by apostles and prophets, who extend Christ's rule into every sphere. Proponents say God works through his people to prepare the earth for Christ.
Raise up kingdom-minded leaders who gain influence at the top of each 'mountain' of culture. Use prayer, prophecy and spiritual warfare alongside excellence in work.
Strongly transformational. Proponents expect whole cities and nations to be changed. Some describe this as taking dominion; others prefer words like influence and reformation.
Proponents say it calls believers to excellence and courage in every career, not only church work. It counters a private faith that leaves public life to others.

Critics, including many Pentecostal and charismatic leaders, say it rests on claimed new revelation, gives undue authority to self-styled apostles, and misreads Isaiah 2:2. Many link it to political triumphalism and say it confuses the kingdom with earthly power.

Proponents answer that 'mountain' language is a picture of influence, not control. They say they seek service, not coercion, and that many critics confuse them with groups they do not represent. Many NAR-linked leaders deny that NAR is a formal organization.
The minas: occupy till I come

Jesus told this parable because he was near Jerusalem and the people thought the kingdom of God would appear at once. A nobleman goes to a far country to receive a kingdom and return. He gives his servants money and says, in the KJV, 'Occupy till I come'. On his return he rewards faithful servants with cities and judges those who rejected his rule.

The parable corrects the hope of an immediate kingdom. The king receives his kingdom far away and exercises it on earth when he returns. The servants trade; they do not reign. Authority over cities is a reward given after the return.

The servants are given real goods and told to work with them until he comes. The Greek word behind 'occupy' means 'do business', not 'hold territory'. Even so, the point is active, fruitful labour now, and idleness is judged.
The talents

A man going on a journey entrusts his property to his servants, each according to ability. Two trade and double what they received. One buries his talent out of fear. After a long time the master returns, rewards the faithful, and judges the idle servant.

The parable is about accountability at the return 'after a long time'. Faithfulness, not transformation of the world, is the test. The joy of the master and rule over 'many things' come after he returns.

The master's goods are to be multiplied, not kept safe. The fearful servant who buries his talent is a warning against withdrawal. Stewards use every gift to increase the master's wealth in the world now.
The faithful and wise servant

The master puts a servant over his household to give them food at the right time. If the master finds him doing this when he comes, he will set him over all his possessions. A servant who says 'my master is delayed' and abuses others will be judged.

The servant's task is to care for the household, which many read as the church, and to be ready. Wider rule over 'all his possessions' is promised after the master comes. Watchfulness is the key note.

The servant already holds delegated authority over the household. Faithful management now is how he shows readiness. The danger is not working too hard but becoming careless because the return seems far off.
All authority and the Great Commission

The risen Jesus says that all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him. He sends his disciples to make disciples of all nations, baptizing them and teaching them to obey all he commanded. He promises to be with them to the end of the age.

Christ has authority, but the mission he gives is to make disciples, baptize and teach. It is a mission of the word, not of political rule. It lasts 'to the end of the age', when he returns to judge and reign.

Because all authority is already his, the church goes with confidence. Postmillennialists note that the command is to disciple 'the nations', and expect whole peoples to be taught. Others stress that teaching 'all' he commanded touches every part of life.
The cultural mandate
God blesses the first humans and tells them to be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth and subdue it, and to rule over every living creature.

The mandate was given to humanity, but sin ruined its fulfilment. Psalm 8 and Hebrews 2 show it is fulfilled in Christ, the last Adam. Believers share in that rule fully when he returns and they reign with him.

The mandate was renewed after the flood and still stands. Work, family, science and culture are part of humanity's calling under God. Neo-Calvinists see redemption restoring this calling; two-kingdoms writers see it as a common, not redemptive, task.
Seek the welfare of the city

Jeremiah writes to the exiles in Babylon. He tells them to build houses, plant gardens and marry, and to seek the peace of the city where God sent them and pray for it, for in its peace they will have peace.

This is a word for exile. Babylon was never turned into Zion; the exiles waited for God to bring them home after seventy years. Christians likewise serve their cities while waiting for the true homeland.

God's people are told to build, plant and work for the good of a pagan city. This is active, faithful presence, not withdrawal. The exiles' peace is tied to the city's peace, so the church invests in the common good now.
Citizenship in heaven

Paul says believers' citizenship is in heaven, and from there they wait for a Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ. He will change their weak bodies to be like his glorious body by the power that lets him subject all things to himself.
The believer's home and government are in heaven, and hope looks to the coming Saviour. The subjecting of all things happens by Christ's power, at his coming, not by the church's effort.

Philippi was a Roman colony whose citizens carried Rome's ways into a distant land. Some scholars, such as N. T. Wright, read Paul as saying the church is a colony of heaven that brings heaven's rule into the world now.
Hastening the day of God

Since everything will be dissolved, Peter asks what kind of people believers should be. They should live in holiness and godliness, waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God. They look for new heavens and a new earth where righteousness dwells.
The present world is under judgment. The fitting response is holiness and readiness, and some add evangelism (compare 2 Peter 3:9). Righteousness 'dwells' fully only in the new heavens and earth.

'Hastening' shows that believers' lives matter for the timing of the end. In verse 10 many manuscripts say the earth will be 'found' or laid bare, which some read as purified rather than destroyed. The reading is disputed. If so, faithful work may have lasting worth in the new creation.
Lord, will you now restore the kingdom?

After forty days of teaching about the kingdom, the disciples ask if Jesus will now restore the kingdom to Israel. He does not correct the hope; he only says the times are for the Father to set. So a literal kingdom restored to Israel remains future and is tied to his return.

Others answer that Jesus redirects the question. He tells them to receive the Spirit and witness to the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8). The kingdom spreads through that witness, which is how the promise to Israel is fulfilled.
Those who expect a future kingdom reply that redirecting a question about timing is not denying its content. Peter later speaks of 'times of restoration' still to come when Jesus returns (Acts 3:21).
The stone strikes the statue

In Daniel's vision a stone cut without hands strikes the statue on its feet and smashes it at once. Only then does it become a mountain that fills the earth. Many premillennialists read this as sudden judgment at Christ's return, not slow conversion of the kingdoms.

Amillennials and postmillennials note that God sets up his kingdom 'in the days of those kings', the Roman era of Christ's first coming. The stone grows into a mountain (Daniel 2:35), which suggests growth over time.

Premillennialists answer that the feet and toes point to a final form of the fourth kingdom, so 'those kings' can be future. They say a growing stone does not fit a statue that must be 'broken in pieces' first.
Your kingdom come

Jesus teaches his followers to pray 'your kingdom come'. If the kingdom had already come in full, this prayer would make little sense. The prayer looks forward to God's rule on earth as in heaven, which arrives with the King.

Those who stress stewardship reply that the prayer continues: 'your will be done, on earth as in heaven'. That is something believers seek and do daily. The prayer asks for the kingdom's growth now as well as its final arrival.
The reply is that both sides hold an 'already and not yet' kingdom. The question is where the weight falls. Most commentators agree the prayer's main focus is the final coming of God's reign.
We do not yet see all things subject

Hebrews quotes Psalm 8: God put everything under the Son of Man. Then it adds that we do not yet see everything subject to him. What we see is Jesus crowned with glory. Full rule over the world awaits the future.
Those who stress stewardship reply that the same verse says Jesus is already crowned. The point is that his rule is real now even when hidden, so believers labour with confidence.

The establish side answers that this is exactly their claim: Christ reigns now in heaven, but his visible rule over the earth is not yet. The text guards against expecting to see it before his return.
The kingdom of the world has become his

At the seventh trumpet loud voices say that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of the Lord and of his Christ. This change happens at the end, with judgment and the rewarding of saints (Revelation 11:18). It is an event, not a process.

Many amillennial and postmillennial interpreters agree it is the end. But they note that Revelation also says Christ already is 'ruler of the kings of the earth' (Revelation 1:5). The final event reveals a reign that was already real.
The establish side replies that Revelation 1:5 speaks of Christ's right, while 11:15 speaks of the world actually coming under his rule. The second waits for the last trumpet.
Perilous times in the last days

Paul warns that in the last days difficult times will come. People will love themselves and money and have a form of godliness without its power. Evil people will go from bad to worse (2 Timothy 3:13). This does not fit an age in which the world is gradually Christianized.

Postmillennialists answer that Paul tells Timothy to avoid such people, so he describes Timothy's own time. Paul adds that they 'will not get very far' (2 Timothy 3:9). The text does not cover the whole age.
Others reply that 'last days' in the New Testament covers the whole time from Christ's first coming to his return. So the warning holds for every generation, and evil and good grow together.
The danger of triumphalism

When the church sees itself as bringing in the kingdom, it can mistake its own power for God's rule. Critics point to state churches that persecuted dissenters, to Münster in 1534-35, and to modern political movements that claim divine mandate. Waiting for Christ to establish the kingdom keeps the church humble.

Those who stress stewardship reply that misuse does not cancel a true calling. Most transformational writers reject force and stress conversion and servant work. Abuses have also come from movements with very different eschatologies.
The establish side answers that the warning is not that service is wrong, but that kingdom language gives earthly projects divine authority. They urge that the kingdom's final form be left to Christ.
The kingdom is in your midst

Asked when the kingdom would come, Jesus says it does not come with signs to be observed. The kingdom of God is among you. The King himself was standing before them. So the kingdom is a present reality, not only a future one.

The establish side replies that in the same passage Jesus goes on to describe his future coming like lightning (Luke 17:24). He is saying the kingdom was present in his person, while its public arrival is still future.
The steward side agrees that there is a future arrival. But the presence of the King means his rule is already active, and his people already live under it and serve it.
Transferred into the kingdom of his Son

Paul says God has rescued believers from the domain of darkness and transferred them into the kingdom of his beloved Son. The verbs are past tense. Believers are already citizens of Christ's kingdom and serve it now.

The establish side agrees that believers are in Christ's kingdom spiritually. It argues that this is the spiritual side of the kingdom, and does not mean Christ's earthly, political kingdom is already established.

The steward side replies that Paul goes on to say all things were created through and for Christ and are reconciled through him (Colossians 1:16-20). The kingdom believers belong to has the whole creation in view.
My kingdom is not of this world

Before Pilate, Jesus says 'my kingdom is not of this world'. He speaks of a kingdom he already has; he admits he is a king (John 18:37). The kingdom is present, though its source and methods are not worldly.
The establish side reads the verse as showing that Christ's kingdom is not set up in this age by earthly power. Its visible form waits until he comes from heaven.

Many on the steward side agree that the kingdom does not advance by force. They say this fits their view: the kingdom is present now and spreads by truth, as Jesus says he came to bear witness to the truth.
Righteousness, peace and joy in the Spirit

Paul says the kingdom of God is not food and drink but righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit. He speaks in the present tense. Where the Spirit produces these things, the kingdom is present and is to be served (Romans 14:18).
The establish side agrees that the Spirit gives a foretaste of the kingdom now. But it says Paul is speaking about relations inside the church, not about society or the reign of Christ over nations.
The steward side answers that righteousness and peace are public as well as private words in the prophets. A church that lives them now is already showing the world the kingdom's character.
He must reign until all enemies are under his feet

Paul says Christ must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet; the last enemy is death. Christ's reign therefore runs now, before the end, and ends with the defeat of death at the resurrection. Believers serve a King who is reigning now.

Premillennialists reply that 'then comes the end' (1 Corinthians 15:24) may follow a gap, as there is between Christ's resurrection and the resurrection of his people. That gap could include a millennial reign after the return.

Amillennials and postmillennials answer that death, the last enemy, is defeated at the return. So the reign of 15:25 must come before the return, which puts Christ's messianic reign in the present age.
The leaven and the mustard seed

Jesus compares the kingdom to a mustard seed that becomes a tree and to leaven worked through all the dough. Both show quiet, steady growth until the whole is affected. The kingdom grows in history, not only at the end.

Some on the establish side say leaven in Scripture often pictures evil (1 Corinthians 5:6-8). Others accept it as growth but say it shows the kingdom's spread in extent, not that society will be Christianized.

Most commentators agree the leaven here is positive, since it pictures the kingdom itself. Postmillennialists hold that 'all' the dough is reached; amillennials say growth is real but mixed with the weeds until the harvest.
The danger of withdrawal

If the kingdom is only future, believers may leave public life, work and culture to others. Critics say this has happened in some circles, and that it forgets the cultural mandate and Jeremiah's call to seek the city's welfare. Stewarding the kingdom now keeps Christians engaged.
The establish side replies that its churches have a long record of missions, schools, hospitals and relief. Doing good is commanded by every view; the debate is about whether it builds the kingdom.

The steward side answers that it is not doubting their good works, but warning that a theology of the future can weaken the reasons for work now. They urge seeing all faithful labour as service to a reigning King.
Pretribulationism is escapism, a comfortable idea invented in 1830.

Pretribulationists ground the view in texts such as 1 Thessalonians 1:10 and Revelation 3:10, not in a wish to avoid suffering. They expect believers to suffer persecution in this age. The origin date is a historical question, and some point to earlier hints (disputed).

Pretribulationists hold that the church is promised rescue from God's coming wrath, which they see in the whole seven-year period. They teach that Christ may come at any moment, and that this hope should lead to holy living and mission.
Pretribulationists teach that people get a second chance after the rapture.
Pretribulationists do not teach that anyone may safely delay faith. Many warn that those who reject the gospel now may be deceived later (2 Thessalonians 2:10-12).

Most pretribulationists hold that some people will come to faith during the tribulation, often through the witness of Israel and others (Revelation 7:9-14). They present this as God's mercy, not as a reason to wait.
Posttribulationists deny that God protects his people from wrath.
Posttribulationists fully affirm that believers are not appointed to wrath (1 Thessalonians 5:9). They distinguish human and satanic persecution from God's wrath.

Posttribulationists hold that God protects his people within the tribulation, as Israel was kept in Goshen during the plagues. God's wrath falls on the unbelieving world, while believers are preserved and then gathered at the visible return.
Pre-wrath
Pre-wrath is just midtribulationism with a new name.
Midtribulationists place the rapture at the midpoint, often at the seventh trumpet. Pre-wrath places it later, after the great tribulation is cut short and before the trumpet and bowl judgments.
